findings.claim: This is why examiners expect you to qualify your answer when explaining cores as a performance factor: “more cores improve performance provided the software is written to use multiple threads”.
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. The spec prints assessment objectives, timings and marks only; it states nothing about what examiners expect or reward. The underlying advice (qualify multi-core answers) is sound, so keep the advice and drop the invented attribution.
findings.evidence: spec sections 2.1 (Hardware) and 3.1 (assessment objectives and weightings) contain no examiner-expectation statements

findings.claim: Examiners penalise the sweeping claim that “more cores always makes the computer faster”.
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. Nothing in the spec supports a stated penalty. Rewrite as direct advice to the student.
findings.evidence: spec section 3.1; no mark-scheme or examiner text is printed in the spec

findings.claim: This exam uses base-2 prefixes for storage calculations. This is critical because answers using base-10 are marked as incorrect on calculation questions:
findings.truth: The base-2 convention is correct and matches the spec (kilobyte = 1,024 bytes, megabyte = 1,024 kilobytes, gigabyte = 1,024 megabytes). The claim about how answers are marked is invented. Ground the sentence in the specification instead.
findings.evidence: spec, Storage requirements: 'the relationship between data storage units using the Base 2 prefixes ... kilobyte (i.e. 1,024 bytes)'

findings.claim: data-revision-tip: 'Cover this and list five characteristics of embedded systems from memory' on a Key Fact whose body reads 'Embedded systems have six key characteristics'.
findings.truth: The lesson names six characteristics (dedicated function, real-time operation, low power consumption, low cost, reliability, compact size). The revision tip should ask for six.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction inside the same key-fact block

findings.claim: Clock speed is how many FDE cycles the CPU completes every second. (Repeated in the glossary definition of 'clock speed', in a knowledge check and in a flashcard.)
findings.truth: Strictly, clock speed counts clock cycles per second; one fetch-decode-execute cycle normally needs several clock cycles. Two options. (a) Leave it: the equivalence is the standard GCSE simplification, the arithmetic in the lesson is right (3.2 GHz = 3,200,000,000), and a student writing it would not lose a mark. (b) Correct it: change to 'clock cycles per second' in the content, the glossary term, the knowledge check stem and the flashcard, keeping all four in step. Recommendation: leave, and record it, because the fix touches four fields and the current wording matches how the topic is taught at GCSE.
findings.evidence: spec lists 'clock speed' under CPU performance without defining it; recomputation of the stated figures shows they are internally consistent
findings.ruling: NOTE: 'clock speed = FDE cycles per second' is the standard GCSE simplification; consistent across content, glossary, KC and flashcard; left.

findings.claim: there are estimated to be roughly 30 billion embedded processors in use worldwide — compared to fewer than 2 billion general-purpose computers
findings.truth: Unverifiable in this session (WebSearch budget exhausted). Published figures of about 30 billion are annual microcontroller shipments, not the installed base, so 'in use worldwide' is probably an undercount. The point it supports — that embedded systems massively outnumber conventional computers — is settled and is not examinable, so no edit.
findings.evidence: no source available to confirm the true value

findings.claim: In your exam, this context may appear in ‘Discuss Impacts’ questions about AI or high-performance computing.
findings.truth: 'Discuss Impacts' is our own internal question-type label, not a board question type; the spec prints no question ladder. Not impossible and not mark-affecting, and the wider question-type relabel workstream owns this vocabulary, so no edit here.
findings.evidence: spec sections 2.1 and 3; no question types are printed

findings.claim: This step-by-step register trace is exactly what exam questions ask you to produce in a ‘trace the FDE cycle’ question.
findings.truth: Names a question type the spec does not print. Plausible in substance (register tracing is squarely in the content), so recorded only.
findings.evidence: spec section 2.1, Hardware: 'the role of the components of the CPU in the fetch-decode-execute cycle'

findings.claim: For 4-mark explain questions about registers ... (same pattern in lesson 3: 'That is one comparison point worth 1 mark') and 1/3/4/6/8-mark tariffs on every practice question in all five lessons.
findings.truth: Unverifiable tariffs. The spec gives only the assessment anchors — written examination 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, 50% of the qualification for the theory component; AO1 30% / AO2 40% / AO3 30% — and prints no question ladder. None of the tariffs used contradicts those anchors or is impossible, so recorded only.
findings.evidence: spec 'Assessment' pages: component timings, marks and AO weightings only

findings.claim: Four-tier ladder 'Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging' on the 6-mark and 8-mark mark schemes in all five lessons.
findings.truth: House wording, not board level descriptors, so it clears the copyright rule and the banned-string list. Flagged only so the unit is picked up by the band-ladder standardisation workstream.
findings.evidence: checker brief, banned-string list (bans 'Level 1'..'Level 9' band names only)

summary: Technical content is sound across all five lessons: register roles, bus roles, cache levels, volatility, SSD/HDD properties, optical capacities and every calculation recomputed correct (4,000 x 3,000 x 24 bits = 34.3 MB base-2; 2.5 GHz and 3.2 GHz conversions; 64-bit bus = 8 bytes; Amdahl 50% serial = 2x), and all 25 knowledge-check answer keys are right. The three real defects are fabricated examiner and marking claims in lessons 2 and 3; one revision tip contradicts its own key fact in lesson 5. No board name appears anywhere in student-facing prose.
